title: The ABC of Symmetric Primitives over Integer Rings: Milk Before Meat
authors: Tim Beyne, Lorenzo Grassi, Morten Øygarden, Berenika Richterová, and Arne Sandrib
abstract:
Designing a secure symmetric-key cipher over a vector space over a field $\mathbb F_{p^n}^t$ is well known and understood by the cryptographic community. Even if the attacks are continuously improving, our current understanding regarding the design and security of the majority of the symmetric-key primitives has not fundamentally changed in the last 20 years.

How does this picture change when we move to an integer ring $\mathbb Z_{p^n}^t$? Although the question is easy to state, it turns out to be far harder to answer. Indeed, there is a significant difference between the arithmetics of $\mathbb F_{p^n}^t$ and $\mathbb Z_{p^n}^t$ and attack vectors do not apply/translate directly between the two. As a case in point, a few ciphers have already been designed over integer rings, yet their initial versions have already been broken.

In this paper, we lay the foundations for a more rigorous approach to designing ciphers over integer rings, noting that this is not only of theoretical interest, but also has concrete applications. We analyze how existing statistical and algebraic attacks will behave for these ciphers and also present new attacks that take into account that not all functions over integer rings admit a polynomial representation. Based on this, we discuss possible design strategies, in which we analyze the security effect of having/not having polynomial S-boxes. In particular, we introduce new properties for the non-polynomial S-boxes that measure their resistance against the attacks presented in this paper. Finally, we discuss how to design such non-polynomial S-boxes, presenting two concrete constructions, and one based on the "digit manipulation".

1     Introduction
The vast majority of the symmetric primitives have been designed over fields.
Whether these are binary or primitive fields is typically determined by the ap-
plication that the designers of the symmetric primitive have in mind. The bi-
nary field allows for good performance in software and hardware applications,
while recent applications such as Multi-Party Computation (MPC), Homomor-
phic Encryption (HE) and Zero-Knowledge (ZK) usually require specific prime
fields, and even more recently, also integer rings.
Integer Rings in Applications. The areas of MPC, ZK, HE, and their
associated symmetric primitives are constantly evolving. While traditionally
defined over fields such as Fp and Fpn , there has recently been a surge
of new MPC-protocols [27,38,32,37,40,63], ZK-protocols [9,10,39,64] and HE-
protocols [34,25,20,21,22,23] defined over integer rings Zpn . It is natural to expect
that the efficiency of these protocols may be maximized with dedicated symmet-
ric primitives defined directly over their respective native ring Zpn , as we have
seen for prime fields. This has indeed also been the case for the HE-friendly
schemes Elisabeth [26], FRAST [24] and Rubato [51].
    An example beyond the setting of MPC, ZK and HE is the tweakable wide
block cipher Mystrium [1] defined over Zt232 , which is currently the fastest prim-
itive on low-end processors that lack dedicated AES or other cryptographic in-
structions, such as ARM Cortex-A7.
    Overall, the design of a symmetric primitive over an integer ring Ztpn is not
only of theoretical interest, but also of practical relevance.
From Fields to Integer Rings. In both the binary and prime setting, the
choice of working with a field guarantees two crucial factors:
 1. every non-zero element admits a multiplicative inverse;
 2. every function over a field admits a polynomial representation.
However, both these two properties are lost when working over an integer ring
Zpn , since only non-zero elements co-prime with p admit a multiplicative inverse,
and only a particular class of functions admits a polynomial representation. An
open question regards the impact of these facts on the security of symmetric
ciphers natively defined over an integer ring Zpn .
   In this paper, we face this problem, and more general, we provide a first
answer to the following question: How to design a secure symmetric primitive
over an integer ring Ztpn ? Although the question may seem simple at first glance,
no clear answer is provided in the literature.

1.1   Security of Ciphers over Ztpn
The properties of working over finite fields have crucial consequences for the de-
sign of symmetric primitives. Most symmetric algorithms are iterated schemes,
in the sense that they are defined via the repeated application of a fixed round
function. The number of these iterations is chosen to prevent all possible attacks
known in the literature, including a certain security margin to hedge against
future cryptanalytic improvements. The main attack vectors against symmet-
ric cryptographic schemes can broadly be classified as statistical and algebraic
attacks. As the name suggests, statistical attacks make use of “statistical proper-
ties” that hold for the attacked scheme with a non-negligible probability. Exam-
ples include linear [67] and differential [15] attacks. Algebraic attacks are based

                                          2
on characteristics related to the polynomial expression that defines the scheme.
Examples include interpolation [54], higher-order differential [57] and Gröbner
basis attacks. By definition, algebraic attacks require the existence of a polyno-
mial representation to work. At the current state of the art, it is therefore not
clear to what extent this class of attacks can be a threat for ciphers over Zpn
that do not admit a polynomial representation.
    The uncertain state of cryptanalysis is reflected in the (few) symmetric ci-
phers recently designed over an integer ring Zq for an integer q, including Elisa-
beth, FRAST and Rubato:
 – Elisabeth does not admit a polynomial representation per se, but properties
   of the underlying non-linear S-boxes still allow for instantiations of algebraic
   attacks over F2 , as shown in [42,4];
 – FRAST admits a statistical distinguisher that may lead to an attack [5];
 – Rubato admits a polynomial representation with error terms, and was broken
   for specific integers q in [44]. As a consequence of this, in a later update, the
   authors of Rubato restrict to prime q, which mitigates this attack.
Both Elisabeth and FRAST argue resistance against algebraic attacks by analogy
with Fpn – see [24, Section 5.1]: “We consider an XOR-variant of FRAST with
addition and constant multiplication over Z16 replaced by XOR and multiplica-
tion over F24 . Such an approach has also been taken for the algebraic analysis
of the Elisabeth cipher ”. Thus the current best approach to arguing security for
ciphers over Zpn can be summarized by the following three steps:
 1. consider an equivalent version of the cipher defined over Fpn (or Fnp );
 2. show that this version defined over Fpn is secure;
 3. claim that the original cipher over Zpn is secure as well.
While this may be a pragmatic first step to argue security against algebraic
attacks, it remains a heuristic one at best. In particular, we remark that there
is no evidence to support the correctness of this approach.
    From this current state of cryptanalysis, we conclude that the cryptographic
community is not able to sufficiently judge (and hence guarantee) the security
of a symmetric primitive over Zq , and it is not advisable to consider ciphers over
integer rings for concrete applications and use-cases. The aim of this paper is to
start filling this gap.

1.2   Outline of the Paper and Our Contribution
The goal of this paper is to present concrete criteria for designing a secure
cipher over an integer ring Ztpn . We start in Section 2 by recalling known results
about functions over Zpn . Next, in Section 3, we outline the high-level design
strategy for the ciphers that we will consider in this paper. As the majority of
the ciphers over Ftpn (including p = 2) are based on the SHARK/AES [70,29,31],
we decided to focus our attention on the design of a SPN cipher that resembles
SHARK/AES. This means that our round functions will consist of an S-box
layer, a matrix multiplication and round-key addition.

                                         3
    For the linear layer, we show that it is possible to deduce bounds on the
probability of the differential characteristic and linear correlations by applying
the wide-trail design strategy to the Ztpn case, keeping in mind that Maximum
Distance Separable (MDS) matrices may not exist over, e.g. Zt2n . For the choice
of non-linear layer, there are three main directions to take: i) a layer of S-boxes
that can be represented by polynomials over Zpn ; ii) S-boxes without such repre-
sentation; or iii) a mix of these two. Each of these options has its own advantages
and disadvantages, which we explore in the rest of the paper.
Are Polynomial Ciphers Secure? In Section 4, we re-visit the algebraic
and the statistical attacks against ciphers that admit a polynomial represen-
tation over Ztpn , first presented in [44]. The idea is to work iteratively modulo
p, p2 , . . . , pn , by lifting the secret key via this polynomial structure. As expected,
a polynomial cipher cannot be secure if pt is too small, as this approach allows
for iterated exhaustive searches.
New Attacks for Non-Polynomial Ciphers. In practice, the parameters p, n
and t are determined by the considered application. If the goal is to design a
cipher over a particular integer ring Ztpn , non-polynomial components may be
required to achieve security. It is then crucial to understand how to choose these
non-polynomial components, and how they affect the security of the cipher. To
answer this question, we need to understand how such a non-polynomial cipher
can be attacked. We address this by presenting multiple attacks, including:
 – probabilistic algebraic attacks that exploit a good polynomial approximation
   of the cipher in Section 6;
 – a new truncated differential attack that works modulo pℓ for ℓ < n in Sec-
   tion 7, exploiting the fact that a polynomial function preserves the zero-
   differences modulo pℓ , while this happens with different probability depend-
   ing on the considered non-polynomial function.
To understand the complexities of these attacks, we introduce new properties in
Section 5 to measure how “good” a non-polynomial S-box is in terms of resisting
these attacks. These properties include the ℓ-Polynomial-Correlation (PC(ℓ) ) and
the Congruence-Preservation Probability modulo pℓ (CPP(ℓ) ). The former can be
seen as a measure on how “close” the S-box is to a polynomial function, while
the latter measures the probability of zero-difference being preserved modulo pℓ .
Designing Optimal Non-Polynomial S-Boxes over Zpn . Putting all to-
gether, in Section 8 we list the criteria that optimal S-boxes over Zpn should
satisfy. This includes minimizing both PC(ℓ) and CPP(ℓ) . We conclude in Sec-
tion 9 with concrete examples of non-polynomial S-boxes over Zpn that behave
well with respect to these criteria, taking inspiration from the the “cut and
sew” approach [44] and the “Kintsugi” one [46] already used in Reinforced
Concrete [45], and its follow-up works Monolith [46] and Skyscraper [18].
Remark 1. Although designing a dedicated symmetric primitive over Ztpn for any
of the applications listed above is out of the scope of this paper, we do believe
that the results proposed here will provide a crucial step towards this goal.

2.3   Cryptanalysis over Zpn

that have not been systematically discussed in the literature.

Integral Cryptanalysis. For primitives defined over large finite fields, integral
cryptanalysis often leads to more significant results than linear and differential
cryptanalysis.
             PTraditionally, integral cryptanalysis is used to find affine subspaces
S such that x∈S F(x) = 0 for a coordinate function F of a cryptographic prim-

introduced in the “square attack” [28] (i.e., by considering the propagation of
structured sets with some constant and some saturated parts), or via a purely al-

Later, Todo [76] partially consolidated the two approaches by introducing the
“division property”, which characterizes structured sets algebraically.
    More recently, integral cryptanalysis has been generalized to rings that are
isomorphic to a product of finite fields by Beyne and Verbauwhede [13,14] (the so
called, ultrametric integral cryptanalysis). However, the ring Zpn does not satisfy
this condition. Hence, unlike for linear and differential cryptanalysis, there is
currently no theory of integral cryptanalysis over the ring Zpn . This issue was
already pointed out in [44, Prop. 1], and it is closely related to the fact that not
all functions on Zpn have a polynomial representation.


3    SHARK-/AES-like Ciphers over Zpn
In this section, we introduce a generic SHARK-/AES-like cipher over Ztpn which
will be the analysis-target of this paper. While we limit ourselves to work on SPN
ciphers to simplify the description of the analysis and the attacks presented
in this paper, we highlight that our results work for other primitives as well
including, e.g., Feistel.
Parameters and Key-Schedule. Consider a prime p, integers n ≥ 2, r, t ≥ 1 and
let k ∈ Zκpn be the secret key. Moreover, let K : Zκpn → (Ztpn )∗ be a key-schedule
where K(k) = (k0 , k1 , . . . , kr , . . .). The ciphers we consider in this work will then
be functions Ztpn → Ztpn given as the composition of r round functions.

Ztpn is defined as

3.1     Choice of the Non-Linear Layer
As recalled earlier, not every function over Zpn is a polyfunction. Due to this
fact, several instantiations of a symmetric primitive are possible. Here, we list
three possible cases, highlighting possible advantages and disadvantages based
on the analysis proposed in the following.

instantiated with polyfunctions only.

that none of the functions S admits a polynomial representation. One immediate
consequence of this choice is that the algebraic attacks over Ftpn known in the
literature would not work directly, as there is no immediate system of polynomial
equations that succinctly describes the cipher.

6.2   Solving the Associated System of Equations obtained via the
      Polynomial Approximation
Rather than finding a good polynomial approximation for the entire cipher, the
attacker can focus only on the non-polynomial parts of the cipher, that is, the

Attack Strategy. A first attempt may be for the attacker to approximate the
cipher modulo pn and attempt to recover the secret key using multiple plain-

    However, a more efficient method is to work with increasing moduli, es-
sentially resulting in a probabilistic variant of the method in Section 4.1. An
extra trick is that we can use information at smaller moduli to filter plain-

 1. the attacker first finds a polynomial approximation of the non-polynomial
    functions modulo pℓ (which is independent of the secret key);
 2. working round by round, the attacker sets up the system of equations modulo

    modulo pℓ−1 ;

    appears the most often among these systems is our candidate for k mod pℓ ;
 5. When k mod pℓ is found (with suitably high probability), the process is re-
    peated for ℓ ← ℓ + 1.

7     Non-Polynomial Ciphers: Truncated Differential
      Attacks
A possible drawback of the attacks presented in the previous section is the fact
that the attacker has to find a good polynomial approximation of the given
function. As we saw, this is not possible in many cases. In this section, we
propose another attack strategy for ciphers over Ztpn based on Proposition 1,

7.1   Truncated Differential Attacks modulo pℓ : Overall Strategy
The attack we are going to discuss can be classified as a truncated differential
one. Truncated differential attacks [57] are a generalization of differential crypt-
analysis, in which the attacker only partially knows the difference between two
elements. In most of the attacks over Ftpn (e.g., truncated differential against
AES), the attacker only knows if a particular Fpn -word is active or not (equiv-
alently, if the difference in a particular Fpn -word is zero or not). We generalize
this approach by considering zero-difference modulo pℓ .
Polyfunction Components. Consider an iterated cipher Ck (·) over Ztpn
in which every component admits a polynomial representation. Given ℓ ∈
{0, 1, . . . , n − 1}, choose two plaintexts x, y such that x mod pℓ = y mod pℓ ,
or equivalently, (x − y) mod pℓ = 0:
 – the round-key addition does not change this zero difference, as x mod pℓ =
   y mod pℓ holds if and only if (x+k) mod pℓ = (y+k) mod pℓ for any k ∈ Ztpn ;
 – due to Proposition 1, this zero-difference is invariant under any polyfunction
   F, that is, x mod pℓ = y mod pℓ implies F(x) mod pℓ = F(y) mod pℓ .

powerful secret-key distinguisher that is independent of the secret key.

S (for simplicity, over Zpn ) of the cipher do not admit a polynomial represen-
